doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Learning bass at the Altamont Hotel and renting basses
summary: Summer 1950 at Tupper Lake the band makes him the bassist; back in New York he rents a bass and tuxedo for weekend jobs.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Greenwell, wonderful tenor player who had been living in Seattle for a long time; and a trumpet player named Marty Bell, who is still around in Florida someplace; and a piano player named John Vincent Brooks, who had been the arranger for Randy Brooks’ band when Buzzy was on that band. Buzzy Bridgeford was his name. And he couldn’t hire a bass player, the boss wouldn’t go for another rhythm instrument. So he goes back up with this quartet, and he tells me when he leaves, he said “look, we’re going to be up there all summer, if things get to be a drag in New York, why don’t you hitchhike up and I’ll put you up for a weekend and you’ll have a nice vacation in the mountains.” So I did that. Actually they had decided to hire a singer and an emcee to go up, and the two of us hitchhiked up there together on the Fourth of July weekend. I think it took us something like 25 hours to hitchhike, because nobody was picking up any two guys with instrument cases. So I got up there and sat in with the band, and faked some three part harmony with the tenor and the trumpet, and Buzzy goes over to the boss and says, “how do you like the way the band sounds? Nice and full, right?” Boss says “yeah I guess so.” He says “you know this trombone player is very much in demand in New York but his doctor found a spot on his lung and he’s going to have to stay up in the mountains for a while. I think maybe if you made him an offer you could get him.” So the boss says “offer him fifteen bucks a week and room and board, see how that grabs him.” It was a Manna from heaven. So I stayed there for the summer. And of course the third day I was on the job I come to work and there’s a string bass on the stand. I said to Buzzy “did you hire a bass player?” He says “no” he says, “I can’t stand playing without a bass so I rented this from a kid that owns one” and I don’t know he gave him ten bucks for the summer or something like that you know. And he says “whoever isn’t playing has to play the bass. I can’t stand this.” So they gaslighted me into being the bass player. Freddy wasn’t interested in it, and I didn’t mind it. It was kind of an interesting problem, you know. And they would take me upstairs and play me records of Walter Page — “Listen to what he’s doing with Count Basie.” Or Ray Brown, “Listen to what he’s doing, listen, try to get that long sound.” They had nothing to tell me about how to do any of this. It was just this is what we want to hear. Which was wonderful. I figured out my own fingering system and the piano player would get together with me everyday and teach me chords, and they would tape record the thing or wire record, I can’t remember what kind of recorder the tenor player had, and they would play me little sections where I actually sounded good, and says, “Now that’s what you—” So by the end of the summer I had found my way around on the thing and was able to play well enough to get by. And when I came back to New York I would go down to Charlie’s Tavern looking for work and nobody wanted a valve trombone player, but occasionally somebody needed a bass player for Saturday night. Of course I didn’t have a bass, but in those days I could run over to Sixth Avenue to Noel

Wolfe’s String Shop and rent an old beat up bass that he had there. He would charge $5 for the weekend. And then I’d run down the street to Jack Silver’s Tuxedo Shop and rent a jacket or a tux for another $5. And the job paid $15, on which the profit of $5 I could live for a week you know?

It was a lot of eating at Horn and Hardart’s. My room on 8th Avenue and 52nd Street was the first room I had, was $8 a week. And then when I found this drummer that was going to the Art Student’s League, he found a spot up in the 80s that was $12 a week that we could split, you know.
